import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 318

*References:*
  - [erdosproblems.com/318](https://www.erdosproblems.com/318)
  - [ErSt75] Erdős, P. and Straus, E. G., Solution to Problem 387. Nieuw Arch. Wisk. (1975), 183.
  - [Sa75] Sattler, R., Solution to Problem 387. Nieuw Arch. Wisk. (1975), 184-189.
  - [Sa82b] Sattler, R., On Erdős property P₁ for the arithmetical sequence. Nederl. Akad. Wetensch.
    Indag. Math. (1982), 347--352.
  - [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
    theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
  - [La26] D. Larsen, [Erdős problem 318](https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-318/blob/main/318.pdf) (2026)
-/

open Set Real

namespace Erdos318

/-- A set `A : Set ℕ` is said to have property `P₁` if for any nonconstant sequence
`f : A → {-1, 1}`, one can always select a finite, nonempty subset `S ⊆ A \ {0}` such that
`∑ n ∈ S, fₙ / n = 0`. This is defined in [Sa82b]. -/
def P₁ (A : Set ℕ) : Prop := ∀ (f : ℕ → ℝ),
  f ∘ (Subtype.val : (A \ {0} : Set ℕ) → ℕ) ≠ (fun _ => 1) →
  f ∘ (Subtype.val : (A \ {0} : Set ℕ) → ℕ) ≠ (fun _ => - 1) →
  Set.range f ⊆ {1, -1} →
  ∃ S : Finset ℕ, S.Nonempty ∧ ↑S ⊆ A \ {0} ∧ ∑ n ∈ S, f n / n = 0

/-- `ℕ` has property `P₁`. This is proved in [ErSt75]. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.variants.univ : P₁ univ := by
  sorry

/-- Sattler proved in [Sa75] that the set of odd numbers has property `P₁`. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.variants.odd : P₁ {n | Odd n} := by
  sorry

/-- The set of squares does not have property `P₁`. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.variants.squares : ¬ P₁ ({n | IsSquare n}) := by
  simp only [P₁, not_forall, not_exists, not_and]
  -- Consider the function `f` that sends `1` to `1` and sends all other numbers to `-1`.
  refine ⟨fun n => if n = 1 then 1 else - 1, fun h => ?_, fun h => ?_,
    fun x ⟨y, hy⟩ => ?_, fun S h hs => ?_⟩
  · have : (- 1 : ℝ) = 1 := by simpa using congr_fun h ⟨4, ⟨⟨2, by grind⟩, by grind⟩⟩
    grind
  · have : 1 = (- 1 : ℝ) := by simpa using congr_fun h ⟨1, ⟨IsSquare.one, by grind⟩⟩
    grind
  · by_cases x = 1 <;> grind
  -- Consider two cases: `1 ∈ S` or `1 ∉ S`. In the first case, the finite sum over `S` is bounded
  -- below by `1 - (π ^ 2 / 6 - 1)`, which is positive. In the second case, the finite sum over `S`
  -- is negative.
  by_cases h1 : 1 ∈ S
  · rw [Finset.sum_eq_add_sum_sdiff_singleton 1 _ (by simp [h1]), Finset.sum_congr rfl
      (g := fun n : ℕ => (- 1 : ℝ) / n)]
    · simp only [↓reduceIte, Nat.cast_one, div_self one_ne_zero, ← ne_eq, div_eq_mul_one_div
        (- 1 : ℝ), ← Finset.mul_sum, neg_one_mul (∑ x ∈ S \ {1}, 1 / (x : ℝ)), ← sub_eq_add_neg]
      apply ne_of_gt
      calc
      _ < 1 - (π ^ 2 / 6 - 1) := by
        have : π ^ 2 < 3.15 ^ 2 := by gcongr; exact Real.pi_lt_d2
        linarith
      _ = 1 - (∑' n : ℕ, 1 / (n : ℝ) ^ 2 - 1) := by congr; exact hasSum_zeta_two.tsum_eq.symm
      _ ≤ 1 - ∑ n ∈ S \ {1}, 1 / (n : ℝ) := by
        gcongr
        have : 1 = 1 / ((1 : ℕ) : ℝ) := by norm_cast; grind
        nth_rewrite 3 [this]
        rw [le_sub_iff_add_le, ← Finset.sum_eq_sum_sdiff_singleton_add h1]
        let S' := S.preimage (· ^ 2) (Function.Injective.injOn
          (Nat.pow_left_injective (by decide)))
        have hS' : S'.map ⟨(· ^ 2), Nat.pow_left_injective (by decide)⟩ = S := by
          apply Finset.coe_injective
          have h : (S : Set ℕ) ⊆ Set.range (· ^ 2) :=
            hs.trans (by simp [isSquare_iff_exists_sq, Set.subset_def])
          simpa [S', Set.image_preimage_eq_iff] using h
        rw [← hS', Finset.sum_map, Function.Embedding.coeFn_mk]
        simpa [Nat.cast_pow] using Summable.sum_le_tsum S' (fun _ _ => by positivity) (by simp)
    · intro _ _; grind
  · suffices ∑ n ∈ S, (fun n ↦ if n = 1 then 1 else - 1) n / (n : ℝ) < 0 from by linarith
    refine Finset.sum_neg (fun p hp => ?_) h
    have : p ≠ 1 := by grind
    simp_all [neg_div, zero_lt_iff, (not_iff_not.2 mem_singleton_iff).1 (hs hp).2]

/-- For any infinite set `A` containing exactly one positive even number, `A` does not have
property `P₁`. Sattler [Sa82] credits this observation to Erdős, who presumably found this after
[ErGr80]. The element `0` is not counted, since `P₁` ignores it, and the infinitude hypothesis
excludes degenerate sets such as `{2}`, on which `P₁` holds vacuously. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.variants.contain_single_even {A : Set ℕ} (hA : A.Infinite)
    (hA' : {n | n ∈ A \ {0} ∧ Even n}.ncard = 1) : ¬ P₁ A := by
  sorry

/-- There exists a set `A` with positive density that does not have property `P₁`.
#TODO: prove this lemma by assuming `erdos_318.contain_single_even`.

The density sits in an existential, so `HasPosDensity` is the *stronger* reading here and
weakening it to positive lower density would claim less, which is the opposite of the usual
situation for Erdős' "positive density". It also costs nothing: by
`erdos_318.variants.contain_single_even` a witness only needs exactly one even element, and the
odd numbers together with one even number have density `1 / 2` on the nose. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.parts.i : ∃ A : Set ℕ, HasPosDensity A ∧ ¬ P₁ A := by
  sorry

/-- Every infinite arithmetic progression has property `P₁`. This is proved in [Sa82b]. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.variants.infinite_AP {A : Set ℕ} (hA : A.IsAPOfLength ⊤) : P₁ A := by
  sorry

/--
Does the set of squares excluding 1 have property `P₁`?

Larsen [La26] proved that this set does have property `P₁`.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.parts.ii : answer(True) ↔  P₁ ({n | IsSquare n} \ {1}) := by
  sorry

end Erdos318

findings.description: The definition correctly requires the sign assignment to be nonconstant on `A \ {0}`, but the docstring says nonconstant on all of `A`. These differ when `0 ∈ A`: for `A = {0,1}`, the Lean property holds vacuously, whereas the docstring admits `f(0) = -1, f(1) = 1` and would require an impossible nonempty zero sum over `{1}`. The same literal docstring reading would incorrectly make the property fail for `univ`. Both discrepancies were verified in Lean; the definition and theorem statements themselves are faithful.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős–Graham, Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory (1980), p. 42, starts with a nonconstant sequence of signs indexed by `k = 1,2,...`, and asks the corresponding questions for other positive denominators. See https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf, printed p. 42 (PDF p. 38), and https://www.erdosproblems.com/318.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to say that the sign assignment is nonconstant on `A \ {0}`—for example, write `f : (A \ {0}) → {-1, 1}`. No change to the Lean definition or theorem statements is needed.

reformulations.difference: The source uses a nonconstant sign-valued function on the set of positive denominators. Lean instead uses an ambient function `ℕ → ℝ`, a global range restriction, and two inequalities against constant functions on `A \ {0}`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Under the binary range restriction, the two inequalities say exactly that both signs occur on `A \ {0}`. Every sign assignment on that set extends to all of `ℕ` by assigning 1 outside it; conversely, an ambient assignment restricts to the source's assignment. The selected sums only involve that set, so extension is immaterial. Lean proofs establish equivalence with local sign restrictions and witnesses for both signs, and also `P₁ (A \ {0}) ↔ P₁ A`.

reformulations.difference: Rather than a negative answer attached to the universal positive-density question, the declaration explicitly asserts the existence of a positive-density counterexample.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Classically, `¬ ∀ A, A.HasPosDensity → P₁ A` is equivalent to `∃ A, A.HasPosDensity ∧ ¬ P₁ A`; this equivalence was proved in the scratch file. Positive natural density already implies infinitude. The source's definitions page explicitly defines natural density, agreeing with `HasPosDensity`; the different interval endpoints affect counting ratios by at most `1/N`.

reformulations.difference: Larsen's Theorem 6 uses a partition into two nonempty sets and asks for nonempty finite subsets with equal reciprocal sums. Lean uses a nonconstant sign assignment and one nonempty finite subset with signed sum zero.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Assign +1 and -1 to the two partition classes. Splitting a zero-sum finite set by sign gives equal reciprocal sums. Both pieces must be nonempty because every denominator is positive and a nonempty sum of positive reciprocals is positive. Conversely, the union of the two selected subsets gives a nonempty signed zero sum. This equivalence was proved in Lean for arbitrary sets after excluding zero. The effective square domain was also checked to be exactly `{k^2 | k ≥ 2}`, matching Larsen's squares greater than 1.

Larsen, D., Sufficiently abundant numbers are pseudoperfect, Theorem 6: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-318/main/318.pdf

Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, and zbMATH 0509.10032 bibliographic records for Sattler, On Erdös property P1 for the arithmetical sequence (1982), DOI 10.1016/1385-7258(82)90026-9; metadata only.
review.notes: All seven theorem statements match the cited source, and their recorded statuses are current. Checks covered empty and singleton sets, exclusion of zero denominators, the nonzero-cardinality condition, satisfiability of the single-even hypotheses, natural density, genuinely infinite arithmetic progressions, and answer polarity. Both scratch files compile without errors or warnings. The squares proof and the proved equivalences have no sorryAx dependencies. The 1975/1982 articles' full texts were unavailable from the publisher; their claims were checked against the source site's explicit summaries and bibliographic records, supplemented by the original problem in Erdős–Graham and Larsen's paper.
